prompt: A consumer packaged goods brand's marketing ROI came in at 1.4x versus a planned 2.3x for the latest campaign. Diagnose the deviation using the channel data given.
context: Channel breakdown of the $2.0M campaign spend and attributed incremental revenue (internal marketing-mix model, illustrative): TV: $900K spend, $1.35M incremental revenue (1.5x). Paid social: $600K spend, $1.68M incremental revenue (2.8x). In-store promotion: $500K spend, $0.35M incremental revenue (0.7x). The in-store promotion ran during a period when a competitor launched a larger, overlapping in-store discount in the same retailers.

binaryCriteria.description: Derives approximate ROI for each channel from the given spend and incremental-revenue figures (TV ~1.5x, paid social ~2.8x, in-store ~0.7x).
binaryCriteria.guidance: Pass if channel-level ROI figures (or clearly equivalent ratios) are shown or stated, not just the blended 1.4x.

binaryCriteria.description: Connects the in-store promotion's weak ROI (0.7x) to the competitor's overlapping, larger discount rather than treating in-store promotion as generically ineffective.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the answer recommends dropping in-store promotion entirely without acknowledging the competitive-cannibalization context given.

binaryCriteria.description: Recommends shifting spend toward the highest-ROI channel (paid social) rather than applying an across-the-board budget cut to all channels.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the recommendation treats all three channels symmetrically.

goldNotes: A rigorous answer computes ROI per channel from the given spend/revenue figures (TV 1.5x, paid social 2.8x, in-store 0.7x) and identifies in-store promotion as the clear drag dragging the blended ROI down from what would otherwise be a healthy mix (TV and paid social alone would blend to roughly 2.0x). It should connect the in-store underperformance to the stated competitive context (an overlapping, larger competitor discount in the same retailers cannibalizing lift) rather than concluding in-store promotion is inherently ineffective. It should recommend reallocating future spend toward paid social (highest ROI) and reconsidering in-store promotion timing/coordination, not cutting all underperforming channels equally.
